why: The contract between the two guards. test_guard.py asserts that the Python removal of each
clause produces exactly the rings this table records, and test-guard.mjs asserts the same of
the JavaScript one, so a case added here constrains both.
The guards exist because a check that has only ever passed is half a check. Each removes a
clause from the library's OUTPUT rather than from its source, because the corpus cannot reach
into either library and must ask the same question of both.
Each clause carries two things a case exercises. APPLIES answers, from the library's own
reading of a model, whether the clause had anything to do in it; a clause is removed only
where it applies, because removing it from a model that never triggered it would measure a
second wrong answer rather than this one. REMOVE is the undoing itself.
THE FIRST VERTEX STAYS WHERE IT IS in every reversed case below. A guard that reversed the
whole list would renormalise the starting vertex as a side effect, the check's ring comparison
is insensitive to where a ring starts, and the difference would therefore never be seen.
Coordinates are metres, and are compared within 1e-9 m because two of the clauses are undone
by a rotation and a rotation through a right angle is not exact in binary floating point.
The base ring is the 4 m by 3 m rectangle in the y = 0 plane that ring_fixtures.json uses, so
the two tables can be read side by side.

note: Measured on the committed fixture with the clause removed: 78 of its 99 surfaces
disagree and the worst is 201.9800 m, which is the x origin of its third zone. The
other 21 are Shading:Zone:Detailed, which a scene reports with no zone of its own, so
the guard leaves them where they are and under-reaches on purpose.

cases.name: a world model is displaced by the origin its zones declare
cases.note: The zone is matched without regard to case, as EnergyPlus matches a name.

cases.name: the origin is turned by the building axis before it is added
cases.note: Clause one runs before clause two, so a library missing it returns R(v + o) while the guard is handed R(v) and can only add. R(v + o) is R(v) + R(o), so the origin is turned first. Adding it unturned is 2.74 m wrong here and exactly right on every committed fixture, all three of which declare World with a zero axis.

cases.name: a relative model is out of the clause's scope
cases.note: The clause has already fired here, and applying it again would measure a double shift that neither library would ever produce.

cases.name: a surface the library placed in no zone is left where it is
cases.note: Site and building shading belong to no zone, and zone shading is reported with none either. The guard under-reaches rather than guessing.

cases.name: a zone the model does not hold moves nothing
cases.note: An absent origin is not a zero origin invented for the occasion; it is a surface the guard has nothing to say about.

note: Measured on the committed fixture with the clause removed: all 34 surfaces disagree and
the worst is 22.5571 m at an axis of 158.434 degrees. clockwise-entry declares 45
degrees and fails alongside it at 5.7100 m, which is the clause doing its job in a
second model rather than a second bug, and the verdict says so.

cases.name: a quarter turn is turned back
cases.note: The clause turns the building by the negation of the axis, so undoing it turns by the axis itself.

cases.name: a half turn is turned back
cases.note: Height is untouched: the rotation is about the vertical, so z is carried through whatever the angle.

cases.name: an unrotated building is out of the clause's scope
cases.note: The identity case, and the one that makes a fixture failing under this guard a real finding rather than arithmetic noise.

cases.name: the turn is about the world origin and not about the surface
cases.note: A surface away from the origin moves as well as turns, which is the whole difference between rotating the building and rotating each surface in place.

note: Measured on the committed fixture with the clause removed: all eight surfaces disagree
and the worst is 4.0000 m. The guard requires at least this, so that a clause reduced to
a rounding difference fails rather than passes.

cases.name: a declared clockwise model is wound back
cases.note: The head is held and the tail reversed: the same ring from the same corner, the other way.

cases.name: the engine's own spelling is matched without regard to case
cases.note: EnergyPlus matches these values without regard to case and the example set holds several spellings.

cases.name: a declared counter-clockwise model is out of the clause's scope
cases.note: The identity case, and the one that makes a second fixture failing under the guard a real finding.

cases.name: a triangle reverses as a triangle
cases.note: Three vertices is the shortest ring a resolved surface can have.

cases.name: what a surface carries besides its ring is carried through
cases.note: The guard removes one clause of the placement rule and nothing else; the parent is still compared.

note: The one guard that removes a clause of the COMPARISON rather than of the resolution
rule, so its removal leaves the library's answer alone and every case below is an
identity. Measured on the committed fixture compared vertex by vertex instead of as a
ring: all 41 surfaces disagree and the worst is 17.5900 m. THIS GUARD MUST GO ON
FAILING; checks/geometry-vertices/check.md says at length why.

cases.name: a model declaring a lower-left start is in the clause's scope
cases.note: In scope and unchanged. What the guard removes is the rotation search in the comparison, not anything the library did.

cases.name: a model declaring the engine's own corner is out of the clause's scope
cases.note: The engine reports every surface from its upper-left corner, so a model already declaring that corner has nothing for this guard to find.
